summary: The talk opens with Romain Huet and Alexander Embiricos addressing over 7,000 AI engineers, comparing the event to a World's Fair where the future was made visible by building it in public. They push back against the narrative that engineering is disappearing, arguing instead that 'AI engineers are eating the world' — engineering was always about solving problems, not writing code, and AI returns it to those roots. They highlight accelerating development cycles: OpenAI went from shipping new models every 15 months to roughly every 6 weeks. They trace a progression from completions to inline prediction, command K, models that test their own work, and now models taking on long, hard goals. Huet shares his Dev Day 2024 experience using o1 preview to build a drone interface — the model couldn't run or verify its code, so he crossed his fingers live. By Dev Day 2025, models could test their own work and control an entire camera and lighting system. Embiricos then shifts to product philosophy. The goal is not to automate engineers but to maximally empower them. He proposes two modalities: chat (which he calls underrated) and a hands-on collaborative UI. The Codex app embodies this — a simple chat interface where you can go as deep as needed. The speakers emphasize Codex is intentionally layered so anyone can build on it. The Codex app uses the same models and Responses API available to developers. New capabilities like compaction are baked into the API first. The Codex harness is open source, and AGENTS.md is the instruction file format. They then introduce App Server — also open source — which unifies control of the harness and is the same path OpenAI uses for its own products. Extensible primitives like in-app browser and plugins (browser use, computer use) are built on the same extension points available to all developers. Role-specific plugins for data science and design are also open source. The ecosystem spans Open Code, Droids, OpenClaw, Xcode, and JetBrains IDEs. Embiricos introduces 'value maxing' — not token maxing — covering cost efficiency and speed. GPT 5.6 Terra brings GPT 5.5-level intelligence at half the cost, while Luna offers frontier-level intelligence at $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. GPT 5.6 Soul runs on Cerebras at 750 tokens per second, fast enough to produce a substantial PR in about 10 seconds. They argue the future should dissolve the local/cloud distinction — an agent should figure out which environment is right. Peter Steinberger then takes the stage, describing his shift from juggling 10+ terminal windows (where he was 'the scheduler, the router, and the memory') to managing a long-running manager agent that delegates to a team. Three changes enabled this: server-side compaction, coordination, and triggers. He traces the bottleneck moving from tokens to compute to attention — the one resource you cannot simply add more of. He illustrates with an automated open-source issue resolution workflow where a manager agent reads issues against project goals, creates workers, runs tests, and returns a PR for human review. He envisions agents that connect to any machine and know which work can be done in the cloud, removing the need to think about where work happens. Steinberger closes by arguing the manager agent should not be trapped inside an app — it should be reachable via Slack, text, or wherever you are, and should design the whole loop for you. He notes that models are advancing faster than the harnesses and organizations around them, making the design of those systems the next great engineering problem — and a call to action for the audience. The future is not 20 terminals; it is better loops.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & World's Fair Analogy
sections.summary: Huet and Embiricos open by addressing over 7,000 AI engineers, comparing the event to a World's Fair where the future was made visible by building it in public. They emphasize the future of engineering is being built by the people in the room, faster than expected.

sections.title: AI Engineers and the Future of Work
sections.summary: They argue against the narrative that engineers are going away. Software ate the world, AI ate software, and now AI engineers are eating the world. Engineering was never about writing code but about solving problems — AI returns engineering to its roots.

sections.title: Accelerating Model Development Cycles
sections.summary: OpenAI went from shipping a new model every 15 months to roughly every 6 weeks. The 5.6 series preview launched the prior week. The progression moved from completions to inline prediction to command K to models testing work to models taking on long, hard goals.

sections.title: Evolution of Build-and-Test Model Loops
sections.summary: Huet recounts Dev Day 2024 where o1 preview couldn't run or verify its own code, forcing him to cross his fingers during a live drone interface demo. By Dev Day 2025, models could test their own work and control camera and lighting systems live.

sections.title: Scaling Engineering Capabilities Through Agents
sections.summary: Agents can now do any task you can do on your computer — not just coding but work before and after coding. Connecting agents to the 'why' and to review/deploy phases enables them to begin and land more work. Codex is used to build Codex. They thank the community for feedback.

sections.title: Defining the Desired AI Engineering Product Experience
sections.summary: With models now smarter than humans on many tasks, Embiricos asks what products should feel like. The goal is not to automate engineers but to maximally empower them. Two modalities: chat (underrated) and a hands-on collaborative UI. The analogy is working with a team — mostly talking, occasionally digging deep.

sections.title: The Design Philosophy of the Codex App
sections.summary: Codex app provides a simple chat interface where you can go as deep as needed. Despite initial resistance from terminal devotees, they argue CLI can't build collaborative interfaces and IDEs start with the wrong order. Codex app starts with chat, then lets you dig in. Community experimentation inspires their roadmap.

sections.title: The Open-Source Stack and Building with API Primitives
sections.summary: Codex is intentionally layered so anyone can build on it. The Codex app uses the same models and Responses API available to developers. New capabilities like compaction are baked into the API first. The Codex harness is open source for inspection and forking. AGENTS.md is used as the instruction file format instead of inventing a new one.

sections.title: Expanding the Ecosystem with App Server and Plugins
sections.summary: OpenAI built App Server — open source — to unify control of the Codex harness, using it for their own VS Code extension and Codex app. Toma (Demilyan on X) built Codex Monitor before the Codex app launched and now works on Codex for iOS. Extensible primitives like in-app browser and plugins (browser use, computer use) use the same extension points available to all developers. Role-specific plugins for data science and design are also open source. The ecosystem spans Open Code, Droids, OpenClaw, Xcode, and JetBrains. OpenAI uses the same systems at every layer it gives to developers.

sections.title: Optimizing for Value Maxing: Cost and Intelligence
sections.summary: Embiricos introduces 'value maxing' — not token maxing. Engineering leaders care about cost efficiency. GPT 5.6 Terra brings GPT 5.5-level intelligence at half the cost. Luna delivers frontier-level intelligence at $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens.

sections.title: Achieving High-Speed Inference for Real-Time Workflows
sections.summary: GPT 5.6 Soul runs on Cerebras at 750 tokens per second — fast enough to produce a substantial PR in about 10 seconds. This enables agents to try 5-6 approaches in parallel and pick the best, making it feel less like waiting for AI and more like a coworker showing results.

sections.title: Future Outlook: Removing the Local/Cloud Distinction
sections.summary: Codex Cloud was the first major launch and is due for major upgrades. The future should dissolve the local/cloud distinction — an agent should figure out which environment is right. Theo predicted this shift; Embiricos believes it arrives sooner than 6 months. They introduce special guest Peter Steinberger, 'the claw father,' who pushed OpenAI to be more AGI-pilled.

sections.title: Shifting from Manual Orchestration to Managing Agents
sections.summary: Steinberger describes moving from juggling 10+ terminal windows — where he was 'the scheduler, the router, and the memory' — to managing a long-running manager agent that delegates to a team. Three changes enabled this: server-side compaction for reliable long-running tasks, coordination for steering projects, and triggers to wake the manager. Persistent context, delegation, and triggers form the loop.

sections.title: Redefining the Bottleneck as Human Attention
sections.summary: The bottleneck keeps moving. Last year it was tokens; then compute (MacBook sounding like a jet engine, fixed by test boxes); now it's attention — which can't be simply added. The most important skill is deciding where to spend it. Watching agents generate code is a waste with latest models that understand intent well.

sections.title: Workflow Example: Automating Open-Source Issue Resolution
sections.summary: Steinberger illustrates automated issue resolution: a manager agent reads a filed issue against project goals, decides fit, creates a worker to investigate and implement, runs tests, another agent reviews, and the manager returns a PR with diff, issue, and optionally a running build via VNC. Paul thought runs a version where his chief-of-staff agent wakes every 10 minutes to coordinate GitHub work. Steinberger envisions agents connecting to any machine, knowing which work belongs in the cloud, dissolving the need to think about where work happens.

sections.title: Closing: Better Loops, Not More Terminals
sections.summary: Steinberger argues the manager agent should not be a session trapped inside an app — it should be reachable via Slack, text, or wherever you are, and capable of designing the whole loop for you. He acknowledges this is unsolved. Models are advancing faster than the harnesses and organizations around them, making system design the next great engineering problem — a call to action for the audience. He closes: 'The future is not 20 terminals. It's better loops. Let's build them.'
